title: Abstract Factory and Builder
scopeHtml: Scope: families of objects, step-by-step construction, variants, and when not to use them.

notes.title: Abstract Factory: the idea
notes.html:
Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related objects through one interface, so the family always matches. Where Factory Method makes one product, Abstract Factory makes a set that must work together (a dark-theme button AND dark-theme checkbox, never a dark button with a light checkbox).

+---------------------+        +---------------+   +--------------+
| UiFactory           |        | Button        |   | Checkbox     |
+---------------------+        +---------------+   +--------------+
| + button(): Button  |        ^       ^           ^        ^
| + checkbox(): Check |      Dark    Light       Dark     Light
+---------------------+     Button  Button     Checkbox  Checkbox
     ^            ^
 DarkFactory   LightFactory

Worked example. A payments module must talk to Stripe or Razorpay. Each needs a matching Client, WebhookVerifier and RefundService. Mixing Stripe's verifier with Razorpay's client is a bug that only shows in production. One PaymentsFactory per provider makes that mix impossible.

Industry examples. javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory, JDBC (a driver gives matching Connection, Statement, ResultSet), Android Material theme overlays, cross-platform UI kits (Swing look-and-feel), cloud SDK region/provider bundles.

Everyday analogy. A furniture showroom set: pick "Scandinavian" and the chair, table and lamp all match.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing it up with Factory Method. Rule: one product = Factory Method; a family = Abstract Factory.
  • Giving a "family" that has no real consistency constraint.

notes.title: Abstract Factory in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: caller assembles pieces, can mismatch them
Client c = new StripeClient(key);
WebhookVerifier v = new RazorpayVerifier(secret);   // wrong pair, compiles fine

// AFTER
interface PaymentsFactory {
    Client client();
    WebhookVerifier verifier();
    RefundService refunds();
}
class StripeFactory implements PaymentsFactory {
    public Client client()            { return new StripeClient(key); }
    public WebhookVerifier verifier() { return new StripeVerifier(secret); }
    public RefundService refunds()    { return new StripeRefunds(key); }
    // fields omitted
}
class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentsFactory f;
    CheckoutService(PaymentsFactory f) { this.f = f; }
    void pay(Order o) { f.client().charge(o); }
}
// choose once at startup
PaymentsFactory f = cfg.provider().equals("stripe") ? new StripeFactory() : new RazorpayFactory();

Kotlin variant:

interface PaymentsFactory { fun client(): Client; fun verifier(): WebhookVerifier; fun refunds(): RefundService }
class StripeFactory(private val key: String, private val secret: String) : PaymentsFactory {
    override fun client() = StripeClient(key)
    override fun verifier() = StripeVerifier(secret)
    override fun refunds() = StripeRefunds(key)
}

Decision gravity. Chosen to guarantee consistency across a family. Alternatives: one Factory Method per product (no consistency guarantee), a config object plus if. Breaks when you add a new product type (e.g. Disputes): every factory interface and every implementation must change. That is the known weakness, and it makes the interface a semi one-way door. Adding a new family is easy; adding a new product kind is hard.

Common interview traps.

  • Not stating the "new family easy, new product hard" trade-off.
  • Picking the factory at every call site instead of once at composition time.

notes.title: When NOT to use Abstract Factory
notes.html:
Skip it when you have one family or the objects are independent. Two providers that do not need matching pieces only need two Factory Methods or plain DI.

Signs of over-engineering: a factory interface with 2 methods and 1 implementation; "future providers" that nobody has scheduled; the factory interface changing every sprint.

Prefer instead: DI binding per environment (Hilt/Dagger modules, Spring profiles) where the container is the abstract factory. Many modern codebases never write one by hand.

Everyday analogy. Buying a matching dinner set is useful; buying a "set factory" for a single plate is silly.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it to model "types of X" with only one product.
  • Forgetting that DI containers already do this job.

notes.title: Builder: the idea
notes.html:
Builder constructs a complex object step by step, so you avoid constructors with a dozen parameters. It gives named, optional parameters and can validate everything at build() time.

The problem is the telescoping constructor: new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null, 2) where nobody can read what true means, and order mistakes compile silently. JavaBeans setters fix readability but leave the object half-built and mutable between calls.

+-------------------+        +--------------------+
| HttpRequest       |<-------| HttpRequest.Builder|
+-------------------+ build()+--------------------+
| - url (final)     |        | + url(String)      |
| - method (final)  |        | + header(k,v)      |
| - headers (final) |        | + timeout(ms)      |
| - timeoutMs       |        | + build()          |
+-------------------+        +--------------------+

Worked example. HttpRequest has 1 required field (url) and 6 optional. Telescoping constructors would need many overloads; the builder needs one required-arg Builder(url) plus optional chained setters, and the finished object is immutable and thread-safe.

Industry examples. StringBuilder, OkHttp Request.Builder, Retrofit Retrofit.Builder, Android AlertDialog.Builder and NotificationCompat.Builder, Lombok @Builder, Protobuf messages, java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder().

Everyday analogy. Ordering a sandwich at Subway: you choose bread, filling, sauce in order, then it is handed over finished.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Builder for a class with 3 plain fields.
  • Forgetting to validate in build() (required fields, invariants).

notes.title: Builder in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: unreadable, easy to swap args
Notification n = new Notification("Order", "Shipped", true, false, 3, null, "high");

// AFTER
public final class Notification {
    private final String title, body, priority;   // immutable
    private final boolean sound;
    private final int retries;

    private Notification(Builder b) {
        this.title = b.title; this.body = b.body; this.priority = b.priority;
        this.sound = b.sound; this.retries = b.retries;
    }
    public static Builder builder(String title, String body) { return new Builder(title, body); }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String title, body;            // required
        private String priority = "normal";          // defaults
        private boolean sound = false;
        private int retries = 0;
        private Builder(String t, String b) { title = t; body = b; }
        public Builder priority(String p) { this.priority = p; return this; }
        public Builder sound(boolean s)   { this.sound = s; return this; }
        public Builder retries(int r)     { this.retries = r; return this; }
        public Notification build() {
            if (retries < 0 || retries > 10) throw new IllegalStateException("retries 0..10");
            return new Notification(this);
        }
    }
}
Notification n = Notification.builder("Order", "Shipped").sound(true).retries(3).build();

Kotlin variant: you usually do not need a builder; named and default arguments plus copy do the job.

data class Notification(
    val title: String, val body: String,
    val priority: String = "normal", val sound: Boolean = false, val retries: Int = 0
) { init { require(retries in 0..10) { "retries 0..10" } } }

val n = Notification("Order", "Shipped", sound = true, retries = 3)

For a DSL-style builder in Kotlin, use a lambda with receiver (buildNotification { sound = true }).

Decision gravity. Chosen for readability and immutability. Alternatives: telescoping constructors, setters, static factory with a parameter object, Kotlin default args. Breaks if the builder is reused across threads (it is mutable) or if build() skips validation. Easy to introduce later because the private constructor hides the change: reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Builder that returns the same mutable object (no benefit).
  • Not mentioning thread safety: share the product, not the builder.
  • Saying Builder is always needed in Kotlin; defaults often replace it.

notes.title: Builder variants: director and step builder
notes.html:
Director (classic GoF): a class that knows the order of build steps for a recipe, and drives any builder. Useful when you build the same structure in different formats (HTML report vs PDF report).

interface ReportBuilder { void title(String t); void row(String a, String b); Object result(); }
class ReportDirector {
    Object monthly(ReportBuilder b) { b.title("Monthly"); b.row("Sales", "120"); b.row("Refunds", "4"); return b.result(); }
}

Step (fluent) builder: each step returns a different interface so the compiler forces required fields in order: builder().url("x") returns NeedsMethod, then .method("GET") returns Optional, then .build(). It prevents missing-required-field bugs at compile time at the cost of more interfaces.

Industry examples. Director-style: DocumentBuilder pipelines, compilers building ASTs. Step builder: jOOQ and some Lombok @StepBuilder forks.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Director when asked for the everyday Builder; mention both, lead with the fluent one.
  • Adding a step builder for a 4-field class.

notes.title: Factory vs Abstract Factory vs Builder
notes.html:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder
Goal Pick which class Make a matching family Assemble one complex object
Result One product, one call Several products One product, many steps
Decided by Subclass or registry Chosen factory The caller's steps
Typical trigger if (type) chains Provider or theme switch Constructor with 6+ args

They combine: an Abstract Factory may return objects built by Builders; a Factory Method may return a pre-configured Builder.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing by name rather than by problem. Say the problem first, the pattern second.
  • Reaching for all three in a 1-hour design; one is usually enough.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Abstract Factory: one interface producing a consistent family; adding a family is easy, adding a product kind touches every factory. Skip it for one family; DI often replaces it.
  • Builder: step-by-step construction with named optional fields, validation in build(), immutable result. Kotlin default and named arguments often make it unnecessary.
  • Director and step builders exist; mention them, but lead with the fluent builder.
  • Do not share a mutable builder across threads; share the finished immutable object.
  • Pick by the problem: which class (Factory Method), matching family (Abstract Factory), complex assembly (Builder).

questions.promptHtml: What is Abstract Factory, and how is it different from Factory Method?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates blur the two patterns. The signal is whether you pick by problem (one product vs a consistent family), not by name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Factory Method creates one product and lets a subclass or registry choose which class. Abstract Factory is one interface that creates a whole family of related products so they always match, for example a Stripe client, Stripe webhook verifier and Stripe refund service together. I reach for it when mixing parts from two families would be a bug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A factory interface has one creation method per product kind. Each concrete factory returns products of one family. The client holds only the interface and never says new StripeVerifier.

PaymentsFactory            <- client depends on this only
  client()   verifier()   refunds()
     ^
StripeFactory  RazorpayFactory   (each returns a matching trio)

The guarantee is structural: you cannot get a Razorpay verifier from a Stripe factory. JDBC is the textbook case: a driver gives matching Connection, Statement, ResultSet.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentsFactory { Client client(); WebhookVerifier verifier(); RefundService refunds(); }
class StripeFactory implements PaymentsFactory {
    public Client client()            { return new StripeClient(key); }
    public WebhookVerifier verifier() { return new StripeVerifier(secret); }
    public RefundService refunds()    { return new StripeRefunds(key); }
}
interface PaymentsFactory { fun client(): Client; fun verifier(): WebhookVerifier; fun refunds(): RefundService }
class StripeFactory(private val key: String, private val secret: String) : PaymentsFactory {
    override fun client() = StripeClient(key)
    override fun verifier() = StripeVerifier(secret)
    override fun refunds() = StripeRefunds(key)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any factory an Abstract Factory; with one product it is a Factory Method.
  • Inventing a "family" with no real consistency constraint.
  • Choosing the factory at every call site instead of once at startup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the factory chosen? -> Once, at the composition root, from config; the rest of the code gets the interface.
  2. Name a JDK example. -> DocumentBuilderFactory, JDBC drivers.
  3. What is the weakness? -> Adding a new product kind (say Disputes) changes the interface and every factory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer defines the UML. A senior states the trade-off (new family easy, new product kind hard) and notes that a DI container often plays this role.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team mixed one provider's client with another's verifier after a copy-paste; it compiled and failed only on live webhooks. One factory per provider removed the possibility.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does the Builder pattern solve? Why not just use a constructor or setters?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you understand telescoping constructors, half-built mutable objects, and immutability, not just "fluent syntax".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Builder assembles a complex object step by step with named optional parameters, validates in build(), and returns an immutable object. Constructors with many arguments are unreadable and swap-prone, and setters leave the object half-built and mutable between calls.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Telescoping constructor: new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null, 2). Nobody knows what true means, and two booleans swapped compile fine. JavaBean setters are readable but the object exists in an invalid state until the last setter runs and can be changed afterwards by anyone.

Builder fixes both: required fields go in the Builder constructor, optionals are chained, build() checks invariants once, and the product has final fields and a private constructor. The product is then safe to share across threads.

Caller -> Builder.url().header().timeout() -> build() [validate] -> immutable HttpRequest

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a builder for a 3-field class.
  • Skipping validation in build(), so you get a fancy setter bag.
  • A builder that returns the same mutable object.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do required fields go? -> In the builder constructor or a static builder(required...) factory.
  2. Examples in the JDK or Android? -> StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), OkHttp Request.Builder, AlertDialog.Builder.
  3. Is the builder thread-safe? -> No, it is mutable; share the product, not the builder.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it avoids long constructors". Senior adds immutability, validate-at-build, and that Kotlin default arguments often replace it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 9-argument Order constructor had two String params swapped (billingId, shippingId) for weeks; named builder methods removed the class of bug.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review of a notification service. Production shows NullPointerException in the sender thread, and one push went out with retries = -1 that retried forever and hit the provider rate limit (about 4,000 retries in a minute for one user).

public final class Notification {
    private final String title, body;
    private final int retries;
    private Notification(Builder b) { title = b.title; body = b.body; retries = b.retries; }
    public static class Builder {
        String title, body; int retries;
        public Builder title(String t) { title = t; return this; }
        public Builder body(String b)  { body = b;  return this; }
        public Builder retries(int r)  { retries = r; return this; }
        public Notification build()    { return new Notification(this); }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with this builder and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, it is a standard builder." Misses that required fields are optional and nothing is validated, so the builder gives the same safety as a setter bag.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are truly required (title, body)? What range of retries is valid? Is the builder ever shared or reused?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix a clamp on the sender: reject retries outside 0..10 before sending, to stop the retry storm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) build() does no validation; (b) required fields are not forced by the type; (c) the Builder constructor and fields are not private.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test Notification.builder().build(): it succeeds today, which proves (a) and (b). Grep call sites for new Notification.Builder().
  5. Root cause: Invariants are not enforced at the one place objects are created.
  6. Fix: Required fields in the builder constructor, defaults for optionals, validate in build().
Languages: Java · Kotlin
public static Builder builder(String title, String body) { return new Builder(title, body); }
public static final class Builder {
    private final String title, body;
    private int retries = 0;
    private Builder(String t, String b) { title = Objects.requireNonNull(t); body = Objects.requireNonNull(b); }
    public Builder retries(int r) { retries = r; return this; }
    public Notification build() {
        if (retries < 0 || retries > 10) throw new IllegalStateException("retries 0..10");
        return new Notification(this);
    }
}
data class Notification(val title: String, val body: String, val retries: Int = 0) {
    init { require(retries in 0..10) { "retries 0..10" } }
}
  1. Prevention: Test for each invariant, make the constructor private so every path goes through build().
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a step builder here; a 3-field class does not justify the extra interfaces.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if validation needs two fields together (retries > 0 needs a backoff)? -> Still in build(); that is the point of a single validation place.
  • Why IllegalStateException rather than IllegalArgumentException? -> The combination of builder state is invalid at build time; either is defensible if consistent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a builder with all-optional fields let an empty Config reach production; the service started with a default empty URL and failed only on the first request at 2 a.m.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: calls the code fine.
  • Hire: adds validation in build() and private constructor.
  • Strong hire: also forces required fields by type, explains Kotlin defaults, and ties the retry storm to missing invariants.

questions.contextHtml: Your PaymentsFactory has two implementations (StripeFactory, RazorpayFactory) and three products: client, verifier, refunds. Product asks for DisputeService next sprint, and a third provider (PayPal) in Q4. Both providers must support disputes; PayPal supports everything.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change for each of the two requirements, and what does that tell you about the pattern's trade-off?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just add the method" with no count of the files touched, or "Abstract Factory is open/closed so nothing breaks".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all providers support disputes, or is it optional? Is the interface public to other modules or internal? How many call sites use the factory?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. For a quick launch I could add default DisputeService disputes() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } and implement it per provider.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) new product kind touches the interface plus N factories plus N product classes; (b) new family (PayPal) touches one new factory and its products only.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compile after adding disputes(): every factory fails until it implements the method. That is the cost counter.
  5. Root cause: The abstract factory fixes the product kinds in the interface, so product kinds are the axis that is hard to change, families the easy one.
  6. Fix: For disputes: add disputes() to the interface and implement it in both factories (2 factories + 2 new classes). For PayPal: one new PayPalFactory and its products; the checkout code, tests of existing providers and the interface do not change. If optional capabilities grow, split into smaller interfaces (DisputeCapable).
  7. Prevention: Keep products per factory small and stable; review any "just one more product" request against the cost of N edits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use instanceof checks in the client to dodge the interface change; that destroys the consistency guarantee the pattern exists for.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Disputes only for Stripe? -> Capability interface or Optional<DisputeService>, not an exception-throwing stub.
  • Would DI help? -> Yes, bindings per provider replace the hand-written factory, but the N-edits cost is the same.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team hit 7 factories and 12 product kinds; every new product was a 7-file change, so they moved to per-capability interfaces and plain DI.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot say what changes.
  • Hire: counts edits for each requirement and names the asymmetry.
  • Strong hire: also proposes capability interfaces and refuses the instanceof shortcut.

questions.promptHtml: Do you still need the Builder pattern in Kotlin? When would you write one anyway?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests language fluency: pattern knowledge should not be copied blindly across languages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Mostly no. Kotlin has named and default arguments, copy() on data classes, and init { require(...) } for validation, which cover optional parameters and invariants. I still write a builder or a lambda-with-receiver DSL for step-by-step or order-dependent assembly, when Java callers need to use the class, or when the object is built over time (a request assembled across layers).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Builders exist because Java lacks named and default arguments. In Kotlin Notification("Order", "Shipped", sound = true) is readable and the compiler checks required parameters. For a DSL:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
// Java: needs a builder for readability
Notification n = Notification.builder("Order", "Shipped").sound(true).retries(3).build();
data class Notification(val title: String, val body: String,
                        val sound: Boolean = false, val retries: Int = 0) {
    init { require(retries in 0..10) }
}
val n = Notification("Order", "Shipped", sound = true, retries = 3)
fun notification(block: NotificationBuilder.() -> Unit) = NotificationBuilder().apply(block).build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Porting a Java builder to Kotlin line by line.
  • Using var properties plus apply {} and calling it immutable.
  • Forgetting that copy() is shallow.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do Java callers use a Kotlin class with defaults? -> Add @JvmOverloads on the constructor, or provide a builder.
  2. Does copy() replace Prototype? -> For immutable data, yes; nested mutable collections still need explicit copies.
  3. When is a lambda-with-receiver DSL better than named arguments? -> Nested, hierarchical structures such as HTML or Gradle config.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "yes, always use the builder". Senior picks the language feature first and a builder only for a reason.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mixed Java/Kotlin codebase had Lombok @Builder classes ported to Kotlin data classes; Java callers broke until @JvmOverloads was added.

questions.contextHtml:
You inherit this class used in 140 places. Two incidents in a quarter came from swapped arguments (connectTimeoutMs and readTimeoutMs both int).

public class HttpClientConfig {
    public HttpClientConfig(String baseUrl) {...}
    public HttpClientConfig(String baseUrl, int connectTimeoutMs) {...}
    public HttpClientConfig(String baseUrl, int connectTimeoutMs, int readTimeoutMs) {...}
    public HttpClientConfig(String baseUrl, int connectTimeoutMs, int readTimeoutMs, boolean followRedirects, int maxRetries) {...}
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it. Which pattern, what does the new code look like, and how do you migrate 140 call sites safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add setters." That makes the object mutable and half-built, and does not fix swap errors reliably.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are required? Defaults? Do any callers pass only baseUrl? Is the class used across modules (API stability)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap int timeouts in Duration to stop the swap bug even before the pattern, if cheap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Builder (6 fields, 1 required) vs static factory with parameter object vs Kotlin defaults (if the code is Kotlin).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count call shapes with grep: if 120 of 140 pass only baseUrl, a builder with defaults changes little for them.
  5. Root cause: Positional primitives of the same type.
  6. Fix: Builder with a required baseUrl, defaults, validation, immutable product.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class HttpClientConfig {
    private final String baseUrl; private final Duration connect, read; private final int maxRetries;
    private HttpClientConfig(Builder b) { baseUrl = b.baseUrl; connect = b.connect; read = b.read; maxRetries = b.maxRetries; }
    public static Builder builder(String baseUrl) { return new Builder(baseUrl); }
    public static final class Builder {
        private final String baseUrl; private Duration connect = Duration.ofSeconds(2), read = Duration.ofSeconds(10); private int maxRetries = 2;
        private Builder(String u) { baseUrl = Objects.requireNonNull(u); }
        public Builder connect(Duration d) { connect = d; return this; }
        public Builder read(Duration d) { read = d; return this; }
        public Builder maxRetries(int n) { maxRetries = n; return this; }
        public HttpClientConfig build() { if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("maxRetries"); return new HttpClientConfig(this); }
    }
}
data class HttpClientConfig(
    val baseUrl: String,
    val connect: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(2),
    val read: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(10),
    val maxRetries: Int = 2
) { init { require(maxRetries >= 0) } }

Migration: keep the old constructors as @Deprecated delegates for one release, migrate module by module with a mechanical codemod, then delete. 7. Prevention: Lint or Error Prone rule banning new multi-primitive constructors. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not break all 140 call sites in one PR.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A caller needs a slightly different config than the default? -> toBuilder() copy method on the product.
  • Who validates cross-field rules? -> build().

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the swap bug had set a 1 ms read timeout in production for one tenant; the Duration type plus builder removed the whole class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: setters.
  • Hire: builder with required/optional split and validation.
  • Strong hire: staged migration with deprecation, Duration types and a Kotlin alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
A PR adds this for a service that talks to exactly one email provider (SES) and has no plan for another.

interface EmailFactory { Sender sender(); Template template(); }
class SesEmailFactory implements EmailFactory {
    public Sender sender() { return new SesSender(); }
    public Template template() { return new SesTemplate(); }
}
class EmailFactoryProvider { static EmailFactory get() { return new SesEmailFactory(); } }

The author says "future-proofing". Sender and Template do not need to match each other in any way.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Approves it because it follows a known pattern, or rejects it with "YAGNI" and no alternative.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a second provider scheduled? Do Sender and Template have a real consistency constraint? Any test needing a fake?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; request changes, it is not harmful in production.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one family, no constraint: the pattern buys nothing; (b) the real need may be a testable Sender.
  4. How I'd verify each: Search the roadmap/tickets for a second provider; check whether Template ever depends on the sender.
  5. Root cause: Pattern applied for imagined variation; the factory interface has 2 methods and 1 implementation.
  6. Fix: Inject Sender (an interface) via constructor and use the concrete SesSender. Keep Template a plain class.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class OrderMailer {
    private final Sender sender;
    OrderMailer(Sender sender) { this.sender = sender; }
}
// wiring: new OrderMailer(new SesSender(cfg));  test: new OrderMailer(fakeSender)
class OrderMailer(private val sender: Sender)
  1. Prevention: Team rule: a pattern needs a named second variant or a named test need.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not delete the interface for Sender; it earns its place through testing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Second provider arrives in 3 months? -> Extract a factory then; with constructor injection it is a small refactor.
  • The author insists? -> Ask for the second variant in writing; otherwise merge the simple version.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite repo had 30 *Factory classes with one implementation each; deleting them removed 2,000 lines and nothing broke.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves.
  • Hire: rejects with the one-family and no-constraint reasoning.
  • Strong hire: replaces it with DI and states when the factory would become justified.

questions.contextHtml: A reporting module produces the same monthly report (title, 20 rows, footer) as HTML for email and PDF for download. Today two classes, HtmlReportGenerator and PdfReportGenerator, each repeat the same ordering logic (title, rows, totals, footer). Last month someone added a totals row to HTML only and the PDF drifted for two weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure this, and which pattern fits?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a Factory to create HTML or PDF." That chooses the class but does not remove the duplicated step order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there more formats coming (CSV)? Does the step order ever differ per format? Who owns the report content?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the totals row to the PDF and a test asserting both outputs contain it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the recipe is duplicated: Director + Builder; (b) Template Method would also work; (c) Strategy for formatting.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the two generators; if only the formatting calls differ, the recipe is shared.
  5. Root cause: The order of steps lives in two places.
  6. Fix: A ReportDirector owns the recipe; ReportBuilder implementations own the format.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface ReportBuilder { void title(String t); void row(String a, String b); void totals(String t); Object result(); }
class ReportDirector {
    Object monthly(ReportBuilder b, Data d) {
        b.title("Monthly");
        d.rows().forEach(r -> b.row(r.name(), r.value()));
        b.totals(d.total());
        return b.result();
    }
}
interface ReportBuilder { fun title(t: String); fun row(a: String, b: String); fun totals(t: String); fun result(): Any }
class ReportDirector {
    fun monthly(b: ReportBuilder, d: Data): Any {
        b.title("Monthly"); d.rows.forEach { b.row(it.name, it.value) }; b.totals(d.total); return b.result()
    }
}

CSV later is one new ReportBuilder; the totals change is made once. 7. Prevention: One test that runs the director against a recording builder and asserts the call sequence. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a director if only one format existed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quarterly report with a different layout? -> A second director method or director class; builders unchanged.
  • Builder holds state: is it reusable? -> No, create one per report.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite finance team had HTML and PDF reports disagree by a rounding rule for a whole quarter; one director removed the disagreement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Factory only.
  • Hire: Director plus Builders, with the drift as the justification.
  • Strong hire: considers Template Method and tests the call order.

questions.promptHtml: What is a step (staged) builder, and when is it worth the extra interfaces compared with a fluent builder that validates in build()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you weigh compile-time safety against API weight, and whether you know the failure mode each one moves.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A step builder returns a different interface after each required step, so the compiler enforces the required fields and their order: builder().url(x) returns NeedsMethod, then .method(..) returns the optional stage with build(). A normal builder catches missing fields at runtime in build(). I use the step builder for public APIs where a missing required field is a costly bug and the required list is short and stable, not for a 4-field internal class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Runtime validation fails at the first run of that code path, which in a rarely used path can be production. Compile-time staging fails the build. Cost: one interface per required field, awkward optional fields (they live on the last stage or on every stage), and every change to the required set breaks callers at compile time (good) and rewrites the interfaces (bad).

builder() -> UrlStep -> MethodStep -> Optional(+build())
             .url()     .method()      .header() .timeout() .build()

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface UrlStep { MethodStep url(String u); }
interface MethodStep { OptionalStep method(String m); }
interface OptionalStep { OptionalStep header(String k, String v); Request build(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a step builder for 2 required fields and 3 interfaces.
  • Forgetting the optional stage can be reached only after all required ones.
  • Claiming it removes validation; value rules (range checks) still need build().

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Kotlin need one? -> Rarely; required parameters without defaults give the same compile check.
  2. Can the required order be relaxed? -> Not easily; staging fixes an order. Use named required arguments instead.
  3. Is it a reversible decision? -> Moving to a step builder breaks callers' code style, but fluent call chains mostly still compile; the reverse is easier.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average has never seen one. Senior names the compile-time vs runtime trade and refuses it for small internal classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A public SDK request builder crashed customer apps at runtime with a missing apiKey; staging moved that failure to compile time.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout service supports Stripe and Razorpay. After a "dynamic config" change that reloads the provider flag without restart, about 0.3% of webhooks (roughly 90 per hour out of 30,000) fail signature verification with invalid signature. Charges succeed. The code:

class CheckoutService {
    private final Config cfg;
    Client client()            { return cfg.provider().equals("stripe") ? new StripeClient(k) : new RazorpayClient(k); }
    WebhookVerifier verifier() { return cfg.provider().equals("stripe") ? new StripeVerifier(s) : new RazorpayVerifier(s); }
}

Failures cluster within 2 minutes after each flag change. CPU, DB and network look normal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the provider or clock skew, and restarts the service.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do failures correlate with flag flips? Which provider's events fail? Are in-flight orders created under the old provider?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze the flag; retry failed webhooks from the provider dashboard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) provider is read at each call, so a flip mid-order mixes the old client with the new verifier; (b) key/secret mismatch; (c) clock skew (red herring: only near flips).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log provider name at charge time and verify time; compare for failing orders. Compare timestamps of failures to config reloads.
  5. Root cause: The family is chosen per call, not once per order; a webhook for a Stripe charge is verified by the Razorpay verifier.
  6. Fix: Build one factory per provider and persist provider on the order; resolve the family from the order, not from live config.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentsFactory { Client client(); WebhookVerifier verifier(); }
class Providers {
    private final Map<String, PaymentsFactory> byName;   // stripe, razorpay
    PaymentsFactory forOrder(Order o) { return byName.get(o.provider()); }
}
class Providers(private val byName: Map<String, PaymentsFactory>) {
    fun forOrder(o: Order): PaymentsFactory = byName.getValue(o.provider)
}
  1. Prevention: Test that a flag flip mid-order keeps the order on its provider; alert on verification failure rate.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the factory global and mutable; a swap while requests are in flight reproduces the bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gradual migration of new orders to Razorpay? -> New orders pick the family at creation time and store it; old orders keep theirs.
  • How to test? -> Fake factories for each provider asserting the same family is used per order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a runtime toggle plus per-call selection caused refund-service and client mismatches for 40 minutes before anyone noticed, because success paths looked healthy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart/blame provider.
  • Hire: finds per-call selection mixing families.
  • Strong hire: persists provider per order, per-provider factories, and a test.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a notification module. Environments: dev (console log notifier), staging (sandbox SMS/email), prod (real SMS/email). The team uses Spring Boot. A colleague proposes hand-written NotifierFactory classes per environment, selected by a static FactoryProvider.get(). Tests currently need to set a system property to switch the factory.
questions.promptHtml: Do you agree? What do you build instead, and when would a hand-written Abstract Factory still win?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the static provider or says "Spring replaces all patterns" without nuance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the environment fixed at startup or per request? Do sender and formatter need to match? Is the module also reused outside Spring (a library or CLI)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fixed per environment: Spring profiles are the factory; (b) runtime per-tenant selection: inject a small registry or Provider; (c) library used outside Spring: a hand-written factory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ask the three clarifying questions; check how many contexts instantiate the module.
  5. Root cause of the concern: A static get() is a Singleton plus Service Locator: hidden, hard to test, global.
  6. Fix: Per-profile beans, constructor injection:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Configuration @Profile("prod")
class ProdNotifyConfig {
    @Bean Notifier notifier(SmsClient sms, MailClient mail) { return new SmsAndMailNotifier(sms, mail); }
}
@Configuration @Profile("dev")
class DevNotifyConfig { @Bean Notifier notifier() { return new ConsoleNotifier(); } }
class OrderService { OrderService(Notifier n) {...} }
@Configuration @Profile("dev")
class DevNotifyConfig { @Bean fun notifier(): Notifier = ConsoleNotifier() }
class OrderService(private val notifier: Notifier)

A hand-written Abstract Factory wins for per-request family choice (tenant A uses Twilio plus its template, tenant B uses MSG91 plus its template) or in a library with no container. 7. Prevention: Ban static factory providers in review; tests build the object graph by hand. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not couple domain code to Spring annotations; the composition lives in config classes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Per-tenant providers at runtime? -> Map<String, NotifierFactory> injected, selected by tenant id.
  • Test overhead? -> Tests construct new OrderService(fake); no Spring context.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team replaced a static factory selected by system property; the property leaked between parallel tests and made 1 in 30 CI runs fail.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: static provider is fine.
  • Hire: DI by profile.
  • Strong hire: separates fixed vs per-request selection and names when a manual factory is justified.

questions.contextHtml:
A batch job builds 10,000 emails reusing one builder to "save allocations". Customers report seeing other customers' CC addresses. Code:

EmailBuilder b = new EmailBuilder();          // fields: to, List<String> cc = new ArrayList<>()
for (Customer c : customers) {
    b.to(c.email());
    if (c.hasManager()) b.addCc(c.managerEmail());
    send(b.build());
}
// build(): return new Email(to, cc);   // passes the same list reference

Logs show email number 4,112 had 38 CC addresses.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix them. Is it also a thread-safety problem?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the mail provider or "a race condition" and adds synchronized.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single-threaded loop or parallel stream? Does build() copy? Does Email expose its list?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the job; privacy incident process, list affected sends; hold further sends.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) builder state accumulates across iterations (cc never reset); (b) build() shares the mutable list, so even per-email builders alias; (c) threading (red herring: loop is sequential).
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test building two emails from one builder; assert CC lists are independent. Check the count growth: CC size grows monotonically, matching accumulation.
  5. Root cause: A mutable builder reused without reset, and the product holds the builder's list.
  6. Fix: New builder per email; copy defensively in the constructor.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
private Email(Builder b) { to = b.to; cc = List.copyOf(b.cc); }   // immutable snapshot
for (Customer c : customers) {
    Email.Builder b = Email.builder(c.email());
    if (c.hasManager()) b.addCc(c.managerEmail());
    send(b.build());
}
class Email(val to: String, cc: List<String>) { val cc: List<String> = cc.toList() }
customers.forEach { c -> send(Email(c.email, listOfNotNull(c.managerEmail))) }
  1. Prevention: Builder objects are cheap; test "two builds do not alias"; immutable products.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add synchronized; it hides nothing here and the bug is aliasing, not timing. A builder with reset() is allowed but fragile.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Parallel stream shares the builder? -> Then it is also a data race; per-item builders fix both.
  • Allocation cost worry? -> A builder is a few dozen bytes; young-gen allocation is cheap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a reused builder leaked recipients across customers in a billing mailer; the post-incident fix was immutable products and a lint rule against fields of builder type in loops.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds locks.
  • Hire: finds accumulation and the shared list.
  • Strong hire: includes the privacy incident handling, defensive copy, test, and rejects synchronized.
